+# Incident Postmortem: High p99 Latency on booklogr-api
+
+## Root Cause
+The root cause was a cache bypass anomaly caused by the introduction of frontend caching (via TanStack Query in commit dc9b248). The frontend started caching search results per user, preventing any duplicate search queries from reaching the backend. Because the backend search cache (`@cache.cached` in `search_books`) was scoped per-user, its hit rate plummeted to 0%, as every backend request became a globally unique query for that specific user. With 100% of requests bypassing the backend cache, each request had to perform a slow (~3s) external API call to `openlibrary.org`. Under typical search typing loads, this rapidly saturated the 4 Gunicorn workers, causing request queuing and pushing the p99 latency well above the 300ms threshold.
+
+## Evidence Used
+- Alert details pointing to high p99 latency (3s) on `booklogr-api`.
+- Prometheus metrics (`flask_http_request_duration_seconds_bucket`) showing 100% of requests for `/v1/books/search` falling into the 2.5s+ buckets, with exactly 0 cache hits (< 0.05s).
+- Metric counts rapidly increasing, proving workers were actively processing but taking a long time.
+- Review of the git history (`dc9b248`) revealed TanStack Query was added, shifting the caching burden to the frontend and exposing the backend per-user caching limitation.
+
+## What was Changed
+I implemented a global (cross-user) cache for the slow external API calls by patching `api/book_provider.py`. The `search` method now directly leverages `api.extensions.cache` to store and retrieve responses from the external provider using a global key (`book_search:{provider}:{query}`). This allows common search prefixes from any user to hit the cache, drastically reducing external API calls, resolving worker saturation, and returning p99 latency to normal levels.
